passage: Friday night. Whole week gone. I was sure I could write a job scheduler from first principles: clean logic, no clutter, no library. Monday and Tuesday were lovely; the core loop was elegant. By Wednesday the tests were failing on things I hadn't imagined: two jobs at the same second, the client's server changing its clock, a job that outlives its next start. On Thursday Nandini glanced over my shoulder and said the standard library handles all of those, and has for years. My face went warm. Seven days for what is one import. I still like my loop, but the release slipped and the review is Monday. Next time, an hour of reading before a week of building. — Chinmay

qa.q: What other approach could Chinmay have used at the start?
qa.a: Chinmay could have spent an hour reading what the standard library does, then built only what it lacked, since that would have avoided repeating solved problems.

qa.q: How might Nandini have seen the situation?
qa.a: Nandini probably wanted to help by pointing out the library, and may also have been concerned that the release was slipping.

passage:
In the one-room software office above the tractor showroom in Hisar, Madhav had not left his desk for a week. The cooperative wanted a tool to schedule tractor rentals among forty farmers, and Madhav had decided to write the whole scheduling logic himself.
"There's a well-known open-source library for this," Nikita, the other developer, had said on Monday.
"I want to understand it properly. From the ground up."
By Saturday he had four hundred lines of beautiful, careful code. On Sunday Nikita tested it with real bookings. Two farmers booked the same tractor across midnight, and the tool gave it to both. A booking during the harvest fair holiday vanished. A half-day rental came out as a full day.
The library, Nikita showed him, handled all three.
Madhav stared at his screen, jaw tight. "A whole week," he said.

qa.q: How many lines of code did Madhav have by Saturday?
qa.a: By Saturday he had four hundred lines of beautiful, careful code.

qa.q: What does Madhav's tight jaw suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt frustrated and regretful, realising a week of careful work had missed problems the library already solved.

qa.q: What else could Madhav have done on Monday, and why?
qa.a: He could have tried the library first and only written his own code for gaps it didn't cover, saving a week.

qa.q: How might the farmers be affected if Madhav's tool had gone live?
qa.a: Two farmers could arrive for the same tractor and bookings could vanish, causing real losses at harvest time.

grounding: It shows a young developer re-deriving a scheduling method himself instead of using a tested library, losing a week and missing known edge cases.
